title: Where Did the Pandemic Hit Hardest? State Unemployment in the CPS, 2019-2026
text:
The question
In the spring of 2020 the U.S. unemployment rate rose more in two months than it did over the entire Great Recession. But a national average hides a lot. A worker in Nebraska and a worker in Nevada lived through very different labor markets. This post asks three questions: how large was the shock nationally, which states were hit hardest and how fast they recovered, and whether a state’s industry mix helps explain the differences.

title: Where Did the Pandemic Hit Hardest? State Unemployment in the CPS, 2019-2026
text:
Data and method
I use IPUMS CPS basic monthly microdata from January 2019 to August 2026, covering about 7.6 million person-month observations of civilians aged 16 and over. Every statistic is weighted with the CPS final person weight (WTFINL), so the numbers describe the U.S. population rather than the raw sample.

Unemployment rate = unemployed / labor force
Labor force participation rate (LFPR) = labor force / civilian population 16+

The series are not seasonally adjusted, so they differ slightly from the BLS headline figures. State estimates are annual averages of monthly data, because single-month samples in small states are noisy. October 2025 is missing because the CPS was not collected during the federal government shutdown, and 2026 covers January to August only.

title: Where Did the Pandemic Hit Hardest? State Unemployment in the CPS, 2019-2026
text:
1. The national shock

Unemployment jumped from 3.8% in February 2020 to 14.5% in April. At the same time, labor force participation fell from 63.4% to 60.1%. That second drop matters: many people who lost jobs stopped looking for work and so were not counted as unemployed at all. The headline unemployment rate therefore understates how much the labor market contracted. By August 2026, unemployment stood at 4.3% and participation at 62.1%.

title: Where Did the Pandemic Hit Hardest? State Unemployment in the CPS, 2019-2026
text:
2. Which states were hit hardest?
The map below shows each state’s annual unemployment rate. Drag the slider or press Play to move through the years, and hover over a state for its unemployment rate, participation rate, and CPS sample size. The color scale is fixed across years, so darker always means higher unemployment.


Code
state_abb <- c(setNames(state.abb, state.name), "District of Columbia" = "DC")

map_df <- state |>
  mutate(code = state_abb[state],
         year_lab = ifelse(YEAR == 2026, "2026*", as.character(YEAR)))

plot_geo(map_df, locationmode = "USA-states") |>
  add_trace(
    type = "choropleth",
    locations = ~code, z = ~ur, frame = ~year_lab,
    zmin = min(map_df$ur), zmax = max(map_df$ur),
    colors = viridisLite::magma(100, direction = -1),
    text = ~sprintf("<b>%s, %s</b><br>Unemployment rate: %.1f%%<br>LFPR: %.1f%%<br>Sample size: %s",
                    state, year_lab, ur * 100, lfpr * 100, format(n, big.mark = ",")),
    hoverinfo = "text",
    marker = list(line = list(color = "white", width = 0.5)),
    colorbar = list(title = "Unemployment<br>rate", tickformat = ".0%")
  ) |>
  layout(geo = list(scope = "usa", projection = list(type = "albers usa"))) |>
  animation_opts(frame = 800, redraw = TRUE) |>
  animation_slider(currentvalue = list(prefix = "Year: ")) |>
  config(displayModeBar = FALSE)






The heatmap shows every state and year at once, with states ordered by their 2020 unemployment rate.

Two patterns stand out. First, the shock was highly uneven. Between 2019 and 2020, unemployment rose by 9.3 percentage points in Nevada, 8.8 percentage points in Hawaii, and 6.5 percentage points in Massachusetts, while states in the Great Plains saw much smaller increases. Second, the recovery was fast: by 2022, most states were back close to their 2019 levels.

title: Where Did the Pandemic Hit Hardest? State Unemployment in the CPS, 2019-2026
section: 3. Does industry mix explain the differences?
text:
3. Does industry mix explain the differences?
A natural hypothesis is that states more dependent on in-person services were hit harder, since restaurants, hotels, and entertainment venues shut down first. To test this, I measure each state’s pre-pandemic exposure as the share of its workers employed in leisure and hospitality in 2019.

The relationship is strongly positive, with a correlation of 0.68. But much of this comes from two outliers: Nevada and Hawaii, whose economies depend heavily on tourism. Dropping them, the correlation falls to 0.3. Industry mix still matters, but it is only part of the story. States such as Massachusetts, New Jersey, California, and Michigan had average leisure and hospitality shares yet saw large increases in unemployment. Stricter and longer lockdowns in the Northeast and on the West Coast, and Michigan’s exposure to auto manufacturing shutdowns, are plausible explanations that this data cannot separate.

title: Where Did the Pandemic Hit Hardest? State Unemployment in the CPS, 2019-2026
text:
Takeaway
The COVID-19 labor market shock was national in timing but local in severity. States whose economies relied on tourism and in-person services suffered the largest increases in unemployment, with Nevada and Hawaii as extreme cases. Outside those two states, industry mix explains only a modest part of the variation, which suggests that policy responses and other features of local economies also shaped how hard each state was hit. For policymakers, the lesson is that a single national unemployment rate is a poor guide to where support is most needed during a sector-specific shock.
Code and data: github.com/Peterjianghaowen/blog3-cps. Data source: IPUMS CPS, University of Minnesota, www.ipums.org.

title: How Far Does Center City’s Prosperity Reach? Mapping Income Across Philadelphia’s Neighborhoods
text:
The question
Center City Philadelphia has changed enormously in the past twenty years. Downtown population has grown, new apartment towers have gone up, and the neighborhoods next to it, from Fishtown to Graduate Hospital, have become some of the most expensive in the city. A common hope is that this kind of downtown revival spreads outward: as the core fills up, demand and investment move into the next ring of neighborhoods, and then the next.
This post asks whether that has happened. Using census data for every neighborhood in the city, I map where Philadelphia’s high and low incomes are, test whether they cluster together more than chance would produce, and look at how income changes as you move away from City Hall. The question matters for policy. If poverty is spread thinly across the city, citywide programs are the natural response. If it is concentrated in a few contiguous areas, policy can and arguably should be targeted by place.

title: How Far Does Center City’s Prosperity Reach? Mapping Income Across Philadelphia’s Neighborhoods
text:
Data and method
The data are the U.S. Census Bureau’s American Community Survey 5-year estimates for 2020–2024, at the census-tract level. A tract is a small statistical area of roughly 4,000 people, which is the closest the Census gets to a “neighborhood.” Philadelphia has 408 of them. I downloaded the estimates through the Census Data API and the 2020 tract boundaries from the Census Bureau’s TIGERweb service, then joined them in R with the sf package.
The main variable is median household income. I also use the poverty rate, the share of adults with a bachelor’s degree or higher, and the share of renter households who are rent-burdened, meaning they spend at least 30% of their income on rent. I drop tracts with no income estimate or fewer than 200 residents, which are mostly parks, the airport, and industrial land, leaving 375 tracts.
Two spatial tools do most of the work:

Moran’s I measures whether neighboring tracts have similar incomes. It runs from about −1 (neighbors are systematically different, like a checkerboard) to +1 (neighbors are nearly identical), with 0 meaning no spatial pattern. Two tracts count as neighbors if they share any part of their boundary.
Local Moran’s I (often called LISA) applies the same idea to each tract individually. It flags tracts that sit inside a statistically significant cluster of high incomes or of low incomes, as well as outliers that differ sharply from their surroundings.

Income is analysed in logs, so a gap between $30,000 and $60,000 counts the same as one between $60,000 and $120,000. Distances are measured from each tract to City Hall, the traditional center of the city.

title: How Far Does Center City’s Prosperity Reach? Mapping Income Across Philadelphia’s Neighborhoods
section: 1. The map: a city of very different neighborhoods
text:
1. The map: a city of very different neighborhoods

Median household income in a typical Philadelphia tract is $62,000, but the spread is wide. A tract at the 90th percentile has a median income of $115,000, about 3.4 times the $33,000 of a tract at the 10th percentile.
The dark areas are where you might expect: Center City, the riverfront neighborhoods north of it, and Chestnut Hill and Mount Airy in the far northwest. The lightest band runs across North Philadelphia, from Strawberry Mansion east through Fairhill to Kensington, with a second light area in West and Southwest Philadelphia. The Northeast, much of which was built as postwar suburban housing inside the city limits, sits in the middle of the range.

title: How Far Does Center City’s Prosperity Reach? Mapping Income Across Philadelphia’s Neighborhoods
section: 2. High and low incomes cluster together
text:
2. High and low incomes cluster together

The map suggests that neighborhoods look like their neighbors, and the statistics confirm it strongly. Moran’s I for log income is 0.66. For comparison, a value of 0 would mean a tract’s income tells you nothing about the incomes next door. The probability of a pattern this strong arising from a random arrangement of the same tracts is effectively zero (p < 0.001).
The local version shows where the clustering comes from. 66 tracts form significant high-income clusters, in Center City, the river wards, and the northwest. 67 tracts form low-income clusters, almost all in North Philadelphia and West and Southwest Philadelphia. Very few tracts are outliers: only 6 are significantly richer or poorer than the tracts around them.
The two kinds of cluster are different worlds:

Within 1.5 miles of City Hall the median tract income is $104,000, and 71% of tracts belong to a high-income cluster. Income then falls fast. Between 3 and 4.5 miles out it reaches its low point of $37,000, and 64% of tracts in that ring are part of a low-income cluster. The inner ring is where the downtown boom has visibly spread, into neighborhoods such as Fishtown and Northern Liberties. Much of the trough, especially in North Philadelphia, is the band of neighborhoods that grew up around the city’s factories and lost its economic base as manufacturing declined. The outer neighborhoods developed differently: Chestnut Hill as a railroad suburb for wealthy commuters, and much of the Northeast as postwar single-family housing. Both have kept a more middle-class or affluent profile. So the map is less a single downtown gradient than three distinct zones, and the middle zone has so far been bypassed.

title: How Far Does Center City’s Prosperity Reach? Mapping Income Across Philadelphia’s Neighborhoods
section: 4. Who carries the housing cost burden
text:
4. Who carries the housing cost burden

Rent burden is high almost everywhere in Philadelphia. Even in the high-income clusters, 41% of renters spend at least 30% of their income on rent. But it is highest in exactly the places where incomes are lowest: 63% of renter households in the low-income clusters are rent-burdened. Because the burden peaks where incomes are lowest, rather than where housing is most expensive, affordability in these neighborhoods looks mainly like an income problem. That matters for the choice between policies that lower rents and policies that raise the incomes of the people paying them.

title: How Far Does Center City’s Prosperity Reach? Mapping Income Across Philadelphia’s Neighborhoods
How Far Does Center City’s Prosperity Reach? Mapping Income Across Philadelphia’s Neighborhoods
text:
Limitations

Tract estimates are noisy. The ACS is a sample survey, and tract-level medians often have wide margins of error. The broad clusters are robust to this, but individual tracts should not be over-read. Some extreme values on the rent-burden map come from tracts with few renters.
Five-year estimates blur timing. The data pool 2020–2024, so they describe the past several years on average and include the pandemic period.
Boundaries shape results. Tracts are administrative units, and a different set of boundaries could shift individual clusters. Significance is tested tract by tract without correcting for multiple comparisons, so a few flagged tracts may be false positives.
This is a snapshot, not a trend. The map shows where prosperity is today, not how fast it is moving. Tract boundaries changed in 2020, so comparing with earlier decades needs a crosswalk, which is a natural extension.

title: How Far Does Center City’s Prosperity Reach? Mapping Income Across Philadelphia’s Neighborhoods
text:
Takeaway
Philadelphia’s incomes are strongly sorted in space. Rich neighborhoods sit next to rich neighborhoods and poor next to poor, with a Moran’s I of 0.66. Downtown’s prosperity extends roughly three miles from City Hall and then stops. The next ring, across North Philadelphia and West and Southwest Philadelphia, forms a contiguous low-income belt that is home to about 280,000 people, nearly a fifth of the city, with a poverty rate above 35% and most renters stretched by housing costs.
The practical implication is that place-based policy has an unusually clear target in Philadelphia. Because low incomes are concentrated rather than scattered, programs aimed at specific neighborhoods, such as job access, transit links to downtown employment, or income support delivered locally, can reach a large share of the city’s poorest households without spreading resources across the whole city. Waiting for downtown growth to spill over has not, so far, reached these neighborhoods.
Code and data: github.com/Peterjianghaowen/blog5-philly-income. Data source: U.S. Census Bureau, American Community Survey 5-year estimates and TIGERweb tract boundaries.

title: How Much Evidence Does a Survey Buy? Confidence Intervals, Coverage and Hypothesis Tests
text:
Code
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(plotly)

# Everything the post shows comes from the analysis repository
base <- "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Peterjianghaowen/blog8-simulation-inference/main/"

key   <- read_csv(paste0(base, "results/key_numbers.csv"))
cov   <- read_csv(paste0(base, "results/coverage.csv"))
small <- read_csv(paste0(base, "results/small_sample.csv"))
nulls <- read_csv(paste0(base, "results/null_summary.csv"))
pw    <- read_csv(paste0(base, "results/power.csv"))
wsum  <- read_csv(paste0(base, "results/widget_summary.csv"))
wpow  <- read_csv(paste0(base, "results/widget_power.csv"))

ks <- function(stat) key$value[key$stat == stat]
ns <- function(stat) nulls$value[nulls$stat == stat]
num <- function(x, d = 2) sprintf(paste0("%.", d, "f"), x)
pct <- function(x, d = 2) sprintf(paste0("%.", d, "f"), 100 * x)
pctabs <- function(x, d = 2) sprintf(paste0("%.", d, "f"), 100 * abs(x))

cov_at <- function(n, level) {
  cov$coverage[cov$n == n & cov$level == level]
}
small_at <- function(n, col) small[[col]][small$n_per_month == n]
power_at <- function(n, delta) {
  d <- pw[pw$n == n, ]
  d$power[which.min(abs(d$delta - delta))]
}
Every month the Bureau of Labor Statistics publishes an unemployment rate, and every month the news reports how it moved. The number is treated as a fact about the economy. It is not: it is an estimate from a sample of roughly 100,000 people, and a different sample of the same size would have produced a slightly different number. How much does that matter? This post answers it by simulation: how precise the rate is, whether the interval we publish really contains the truth, and what a smaller survey would have concluded.
The data are the IPUMS Current Population Survey basic monthly microdata, January 2019 to August 2026. I compare January 2019 with January 2024 — the same month in different years, so the labour market’s seasonal pattern cancels out — and ask whether the unemployment rate really changed. It was 4.47% in January 2019 (97,181 people) and 4.12% in January 2024 (80,923 people): a fall of 0.35 percentage points. Is that a change in the economy, or a change in who answered the phone?

title: How Much Evidence Does a Survey Buy? Confidence Intervals, Coverage and Hypothesis Tests
text:
1. Build the interval by resampling
The usual way to put an interval around an estimate is a formula that assumes the sample was drawn at random from a population of equal-weight people. The CPS is neither simple nor equal-weighted — its final person weights run from 177 to 13,140 — so we resample instead: draw the same number of interviewed people at random with replacement, recompute the weighted rate, and repeat 2,000 times. The spread of those 2,000 numbers is the bootstrap distribution: how much the estimate would have moved if we had interviewed somebody else.



Bootstrap distributions of the January 2024 rate and of the change from January 2019.


The bootstrap interval for January 2024 is 3.92% to 4.32%, and for the change between the two months -0.64 to -0.08 percentage points. The textbook interval for the same change is -0.54 to -0.16 — 49% narrower. That gap is a design effect: the textbook formula understates the real sampling error of the CPS by almost half, so every interval built that way is too narrow.

title: How Much Evidence Does a Survey Buy? Confidence Intervals, Coverage and Hypothesis Tests
section: 2. Does a 95% interval contain the truth 95% of the time?
text:
2. Does a 95% interval contain the truth 95% of the time?
An interval is a promise about how often it will contain the truth, and promises should be checked: build a population with a known unemployment rate, sample it over and over, and count how often the interval contains the truth.



Simulated coverage of the interval, and coverage on the real CPS data.


The promise is kept: at 95%, coverage is 93.2% with 250 interviews and 95.0% with 80,923, and every other nominal level lands within about a point of what it promised.
The same test on the real CPS data is less comfortable. Repeating the experiment 1,000 times with smaller surveys, the bootstrap interval contains the full-sample estimate about 92% of the time; the textbook interval about 80% of the time. The bootstrap is at least honest about a weighted proportion being a lopsided statistic. The formula is not.

title: How Much Evidence Does a Survey Buy? Confidence Intervals, Coverage and Hypothesis Tests
section: 3. A p-value is an area under a simulated null distribution
text:
3. A p-value is an area under a simulated null distribution
To say “the rate changed”, we test H0: the two months have the same rate. Under H0 the estimated change is still random, with a distribution centred on zero. Simulating that experiment 20,000 times gives the null distribution below; everything outside ±0.29 points is the rejection region, 5% of the null distribution by construction.



The simulated null distribution of the estimated change, with the rejection region and the observed change.


The observed change of -0.35 points falls just inside that region, and the p-value is simply the area of the null distribution beyond what we observed: 0.016. The textbook formula, using the too-small standard error, would have said 0.014. Both are correct arithmetic; only one is honest about how much the estimate can move.

title: How Much Evidence Does a Survey Buy? Confidence Intervals, Coverage and Hypothesis Tests
section: 4. How much could this survey have found?
text:
4. How much could this survey have found?
The most useful thing a simulation tells you is what a survey could have found. The power to detect the change we measured rises from 5.8% with 1,000 interviews per month to 66.8% with 80,923.



Power curves: the chance of detecting a real change at different sample sizes.


The interactive figure below puts that in your hands: drag the slider to change how many people were interviewed each month, and watch the statistic move, the p-value fall, and the verdict flip.


Code
z_grid <- seq(-4, 4, length.out = 401)
crit_z <- 1.96

xl <- seq(-4, -crit_z, length.out = 120)
xr <- seq(4, crit_z, length.out = 120)
left_x  <- c(xl, -crit_z, -4);  left_y  <- c(dnorm(xl), 0, 0)
right_x <- c(xr, crit_z, 4);   right_y <- c(dnorm(xr), 0, 0)

power_grid <- sort(unique(wpow$delta)) * 100          # percentage points
power_y <- lapply(wsum$n, function(n) {
  p <- wpow$power[wpow$n == n]
  approx(sort(unique(wpow$delta)) * 100, p, xout = power_grid)$y
})

label_for <- function(i) {
  sprintf("n = %s per month<br>z = %+.2f  |  p-value = %s<br>%s",
          format(wsum$n[i], big.mark = ","), wsum$z_obs[i],
          ifelse(wsum$p_value[i] < 0.001, "< 0.001", sprintf("%.3f", wsum$p_value[i])),
          ifelse(wsum$p_value[i] < 0.05,
                 "reject H0: the rate really changed",
                 "cannot reject H0: not enough evidence"))
}

p <- p |> add_trace(
  x = z_grid, y = dnorm(z_grid), type = "scatter", mode = "lines",
  line = list(color = "#1f77b4", width = 2), fill = "tozeroy",
  fillcolor = "rgba(31,119,180,0.18)", hoverinfo = "skip", showlegend = FALSE,
  xaxis = "x", yaxis = "y")

  x = left_x, y = left_y, type = "scatter", mode = "lines", fill = "toself",
  fillcolor = "rgba(214,39,40,0.18)", line = list(width = 0), hoverinfo = "skip",

title: How Much Evidence Does a Survey Buy? Confidence Intervals, Coverage and Hypothesis Tests
text:
Takeaway
A confidence interval and a p-value are statements about the data you happened to collect, not about the world. The bootstrap says how much your estimate would move if you collected slightly different data; simulation says how often the interval you built would have been right; and the null distribution turns “significant” into a tail area you can point at. None of this replaces judgement, but it puts a number on the part of a conclusion that came from luck.
The unemployment rate fell by 0.35 points between January 2019 and January 2024, and this sample is large enough to notice it: the 95% interval runs from -0.64 to -0.08 points, and the simulated p-value is 0.016. The same comparison in a survey a tenth the size would have been indistinguishable from noise — and a confident headline would have said nothing changed. Simulation is what tells the two apart.
Code and data: github.com/Peterjianghaowen/blog8-simulation-inference. Data source: IPUMS Current Population Survey, University of Minnesota.

title: One Theorem, Four Lemmas: The Envelope Theorem in Microeconomics
text:
Suppose the price of gasoline rises from $3.00 to $3.10 a gallon. How much worse off are you?
The honest answer seems to require a lot of work. You might drive a little less, combine errands, or take the bus once a week. To measure the damage properly you would have to work out how you re-optimise your whole budget at the new price, then compare.
The envelope theorem says you can skip all of that. For a small price change, the damage is simply
\[\text{loss} \approx (\text{gallons you currently buy}) \times (\text{price increase}).\]
If you buy 40 gallons a month, a 10-cent rise costs you about $4 a month, whatever you end up doing about it.
This matters for two reasons. First, it is how economists price small policy changes in practice. Estimating the cost of a new tax, or a firm’s exposure to a wage rise, rarely requires a model of how everyone will substitute; current quantities are enough. Second, intermediate microeconomics teaches four results as if they were separate facts: Shephard’s Lemma, Hotelling’s Lemma, Roy’s Identity and the Le Chatelier principle. Each has its own proof. This post argues that all four are the gasoline calculation above, applied to different problems, and that once you see this you only need to remember one idea.

title: One Theorem, Four Lemmas: The Envelope Theorem in Microeconomics
section: The intuition: the top of a hill is flat
text:
The intuition: the top of a hill is flat
You have already chosen the best bundle at the current prices. That means you are at the top of a hill: every small change to your choices, such as one gallon more or less, leaves you no better off.
When the price moves, two things happen:

Direct effect. The bundle you already hold becomes more expensive. This is the 40 gallons × 10 cents.
Indirect effect. You re-optimise, shifting your choices to the new best bundle.

The indirect effect is a small movement away from the top of the hill. At the top, the ground is flat, so a small step changes your height by almost nothing. That is why the indirect effect can be ignored for small changes, and why only the direct effect is left. The rest of the post is this sentence written in different notation.

title: One Theorem, Four Lemmas: The Envelope Theorem in Microeconomics
text:
Checking it with numbers
Before the general proof, it is worth confirming that the shortcut actually works. Take a consumer with Cobb-Douglas utility \(u(x_1,x_2) = x_1^{0.5}x_2^{0.5}\) who needs to reach utility \(\bar u = 1\), with \(p_2 = 1\). At \(p_1 = 1\) she buys one unit of good 1. The code below raises \(p_1\) by different amounts and compares two numbers:

Exact: the true extra spending needed to stay equally well off, after she fully re-optimises.
Shortcut: current quantity × price change, ignoring any re-optimisation.



Show code
a <- 0.5; u_bar <- 1; p2 <- 1; p0 <- 1

# Expenditure function for Cobb-Douglas (closed form)
e <- function(p1) u_bar * (p1 / a)^a * (p2 / (1 - a))^(1 - a)
x1_now <- a * e(p0) / p0          # quantity of good 1 bought at p0

dp <- c(0.01, 0.05, 0.10, 0.25, 0.50, 1.00)
check <- data.frame(
  rise     = dp,
  exact    = e(p0 + dp) - e(p0),
  shortcut = x1_now * dp
)
check$error_pct <- 100 * (check$shortcut - check$exact) / check$exact

knitr::kable(check, digits = c(2, 4, 4, 1),

For a 1% price rise the shortcut is off by about a quarter of a percent. For a 10% rise it is off by about 2%. Only when the price doubles does the error become large, about 20%. Two things stand out:

The shortcut always overstates the cost. It assumes she keeps buying the old bundle, when in fact she can substitute toward the cheaper good and soften the blow.
The dollar gap between the two grows with the square of the price change. Doubling the price rise roughly quadruples the gap (and doubles the percentage error). That is the “flat top of the hill” in numbers: the benefit of re-optimising is a second-order effect.

The same logic explains a well-known problem with official inflation measures. A fixed-basket price index like the CPI uses the shortcut: it prices last period’s basket at this period’s prices. As the table shows, that overstates how much more it costs to stay equally well off, and the bias is larger when prices move a lot. This is the “substitution bias” in the CPI.

title: One Theorem, Four Lemmas: The Envelope Theorem in Microeconomics
text:
The general result
Now the same argument in symbols. Let \(f(x,\theta)\) be what we are maximising (utility, profit), \(x\) the choice, and \(\theta\) a parameter we do not control (a price). Write \(x^*(\theta)\) for the best choice and \(V(\theta) = f(x^*(\theta),\theta)\) for the best achievable value. By the chain rule,
\[\frac{dV}{d\theta} = \underbrace{\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\bigg|_{x^*}\frac{dx^*}{d\theta}}_{\text{indirect: re-optimising}} \;+\; \underbrace{\frac{\partial f}{\partial \theta}\bigg|_{x^*}}_{\text{direct}}.\]
At the optimum the first-order condition says \(\partial f/\partial x = 0\), which is the flat hilltop. So the indirect term vanishes and
\[\boxed{\;\frac{dV}{d\theta} = \frac{\partial f}{\partial \theta}\bigg|_{x = x^*(\theta)}\;}\]
Notice what we never had to compute: \(dx^*/d\theta\), how the choice responds. That is often the hardest part of a problem, and the theorem lets us avoid it.
With a budget or other constraint. Most economic problems have a constraint, \(g(x,\theta) = 0\), and then \(\partial f/\partial x\) is not zero at the optimum, because you are pushed against the constraint rather than sitting on a free hilltop. The fix is to include the constraint in the objective with a Lagrange multiplier \(\lambda\), \(\mathcal{L} = f - \lambda g\). The Lagrangian is flat at the optimum in exactly the way \(f\) was before, so the same argument goes through:
\[\frac{dV}{d\theta} = \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \theta}\bigg|_{x^*,\,\lambda^*} = \frac{\partial f}{\partial \theta} - \lambda^* \frac{\partial g}{\partial \theta}.\]
In words: differentiate the Lagrangian with respect to the parameter and hold everything else fixed. The second term has a clean meaning. \(\lambda^*\) is the value of relaxing the constraint by one unit, so if the parameter also tightens the constraint, that cost is priced at \(\lambda^*\). The same result holds for minimisation problems, since minimising \(f\) is the same as maximising \(-f\).

title: One Theorem, Four Lemmas: The Envelope Theorem in Microeconomics
text:
Four lemmas, one idea
Each famous result below is one application of the boxed formula. In every case the recipe is the same: write down the problem, pick the price that changes, and ask, “If I hold my current choices fixed, how much does this price change cost or earn me?” The table summarises; the paragraphs explain what each result means.










Result
Problem
Price that changes
Direct effect, holding choices fixed
Conclusion




Shephard’s Lemma
Minimise spending to reach utility \(\bar u\)
Price of good \(i\)
You pay extra on each unit you buy
\(\partial e/\partial p_i = h_i\)


Hotelling’s Lemma
Maximise profit
Output price \(p\)
You earn extra on each unit you sell
\(\partial \pi/\partial p = y^*\)


Roy’s Identity
Maximise utility with income \(m\)
Price of good \(i\)
Like losing income equal to \(x_i\)
\(x_i^* = -\dfrac{\partial v/\partial p_i}{\partial v/\partial m}\)


Le Chatelier
Minimise cost, short run vs long run
Input price \(w_1\)
Same, but one problem has fewer choices
Long-run demand responds more



Shephard’s Lemma is the gasoline example. The expenditure function \(e(p,\bar u)\) is the least you can spend to reach utility \(\bar u\). Raise \(p_i\) by a dollar while keeping your bundle fixed and your bill rises by \(h_i\), the number of units you buy. So
\[\frac{\partial e}{\partial p_i} = h_i(p,\bar u).\]
The practical reading: the slope of the cost-of-living function with respect to a price is your consumption of that good. Applied to a firm’s cost function it gives \(\partial c/\partial w_j = x_j\): a $1 wage rise increases costs by the number of hours currently employed.
Hotelling’s Lemma is the same calculation for a firm maximising profit \(\pi(p,w) = \max_x \{p\,F(x) - w\cdot x\}\). If the output price rises by a dollar and the firm changes nothing, profit rises by one dollar per unit produced:
\[\frac{\partial \pi}{\partial p} = y^*(p,w), \qquad \frac{\partial \pi}{\partial w_j} = -x_j^*(p,w).\]
The firm will also expand output in response, but by the flat-hilltop argument that adjustment adds nothing at the margin.
Roy’s Identity looks the most mysterious, but it is the same idea plus a conversion of units. The indirect utility function \(v(p,m)\) gives the best utility reachable with prices \(p\) and income \(m\). A rise in \(p_i\), holding the bundle fixed, takes away \(x_i\) dollars of purchasing power, exactly like an income loss of \(x_i\). So
\[\frac{\partial v}{\partial p_i} = -\lambda\, x_i^*, \qquad \frac{\partial v}{\partial m} = \lambda,\]
where \(\lambda\) is the utility value of one extra dollar. Dividing the two converts utility back into dollars, and \(\lambda\) cancels:
\[x_i^*(p,m) = -\frac{\partial v/\partial p_i}{\partial v/\partial m}.\]
The useful part: if you know how well-being depends on prices and income, you can read off demand without solving the consumer’s problem again.
The Le Chatelier principle asks how a firm’s demand for an input responds to its price in the short run, when another input \(x_2\) is fixed, compared with the long run, when it can adjust. Both cost functions satisfy Shephard’s Lemma, so both slopes equal the quantity demanded at the reference price, and the two cost curves touch there. Away from that point, the long-run firm can do everything the short-run firm can and more, so its costs are weakly lower: the long-run cost curve is the envelope of the short-run ones. Two curves that touch, with one always below the other, must have the lower one bending more sharply. Translating curvature into demand slopes gives
\[\left|\frac{\partial x_1^{\mathrm{LR}}}{\partial w_1}\right| \ \ge\ \left|\frac{\partial x_1^{\mathrm{SR}}}{\partial w_1}\right|.\]
In plain terms: more flexibility means a bigger response to prices. This is why demand for energy, or for labour, is usually estimated to be more elastic over several years than over a few months.
Why they are the same. In all four cases the answer comes from the direct effect alone, because the agent is already at an optimum and small re-adjustments are worth nothing to first order. The lemmas differ only in which problem they apply to and which price is changing.

title: One Theorem, Four Lemmas: The Envelope Theorem in Microeconomics
text:
Why “envelope”?
The name comes from a picture. Fix any bundle and ask how much it costs as \(p_1\) changes. The answer is a straight line, because you are buying fixed quantities. Every bundle gives a different line. Someone who re-optimises at every price always picks the cheapest of these lines, so their spending traces out the lower envelope of the whole family.


Show code
library(ggplot2)

h1 <- function(p1) a * e(p1) / p1
p_grid <- seq(0.5, 4, length.out = 200)

fixed_bundle_line <- function(p_anchor) {
  x1 <- h1(p_anchor)
  x2 <- (1 - a) * e(p_anchor) / p2
  data.frame(p1 = p_grid, cost = p_grid * x1 + p2 * x2, anchor = p_anchor)
}

lines_df <- do.call(rbind, lapply(c(0.75, 1.25, 2, 3), fixed_bundle_line))
env_df   <- data.frame(p1 = p_grid, cost = e(p_grid))
touch_df <- data.frame(p1 = c(0.75, 1.25, 2, 3), cost = e(c(0.75, 1.25, 2, 3)))

ggplot() +
  geom_line(data = lines_df, aes(p1, cost, group = anchor),
            colour = "grey65", linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_line(data = env_df, aes(p1, cost), linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(data = touch_df, aes(p1, cost), size = 2) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 6)) +
  labs(x = expression("Price of good 1, " * p[1]),
       y = "Spending needed to reach utility 1") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)








Figure 1: Grey lines: the cost of keeping one fixed bundle as the price of good 1 changes. Black curve: the cost when the consumer re-optimises at every price. The black curve is the lower envelope of the grey lines and touches each one at the price where that bundle is optimal.





Three features of the chart are the theory in visual form:

The lines touch the curve rather than cross it. At each dot the fixed bundle is the optimal one, so the line and the curve have the same slope. The slope of a grey line is the quantity of good 1 in that bundle, so the slope of the expenditure function equals current consumption. That is Shephard’s Lemma.
The grey lines lie above the curve everywhere else. Keeping a fixed bundle can never be cheaper than re-optimising. This is why the shortcut in the table always overstated the cost, and why the CPI’s fixed basket overstates inflation.
The gap opens slowly near each dot. Close to the touching point, the line and the curve are almost indistinguishable, and the gap widens with the square of the distance. That is the “error grows with the square” pattern in the table.

Data. No external data. All numbers and curves are generated from the closed-form Cobb-Douglas expenditure function in the code above, with \(a = 0.5\), \(\bar u = 1\) and \(p_2 = 1\).

title: One Theorem, Four Lemmas: The Envelope Theorem in Microeconomics
text:
Takeaway
When a price or other parameter changes by a small amount, the effect on an optimised outcome is just the direct effect on what you are currently doing: current quantity times the price change. You do not need to know how people or firms will adjust, because at an optimum small adjustments are worth nothing to first order. That one idea is Shephard’s Lemma, Hotelling’s Lemma, Roy’s Identity and the Le Chatelier principle.
The practical rule and its limit go together. For small changes, such as a modest tax or a 5% price rise, current quantities give a reliable estimate. For large changes the shortcut overstates the cost, because people do substitute, and the error grows quickly. In those cases you need to model behaviour, and the difference between the two answers is a measure of how much substitution is worth.

title: How Much of a Parent’s Success Does a Child Inherit? Matching Parents and Children with SQL
text:
The question
How much of a parent’s economic position does a child inherit? The intergenerational income elasticity (IGE) compresses the answer into a single number: the percentage change in a child’s income associated with a 1% change in their parent’s income. An IGE of 0.30 means a family whose income is 10% above average produces a child whose income is roughly 3% above average.
It is one of the most stable facts in economics, and one of the most policy-relevant, because it sets the ceiling on how far inequality can move between generations. If persistence is high, then the starting position of a child’s parents does a great deal of work in determining where the child ends up, and policy that treats markets as the efficient solver of income distribution has to be reconsidered.
Measuring it is harder than it looks. Parents and children have to be matched across decades of panel data. Their incomes have to be measured in a way that is not distorted by a single good or bad year. And the child’s age has to be chosen carefully, because a 28-year-old’s income is not yet their long-run income. This post does the matching with SQL, which turns out to be a natural fit: a JOIN on identifiers, a GROUP BY on the child, and an AVG() over the matched parents.

title: How Much of a Parent’s Success Does a Child Inherit? Matching Parents and Children with SQL
text:
Data and method
The data are the Panel Study of Income Dynamics (PSID), the long-running panel of the Institute for Social Research at the University of Michigan. Since 1968 the study has re-interviewed the same families, and most of the same people, every year. Two files are needed:

The 2023 individual and family file, downloaded from the PSID Data Center with the variables for family income in 2020 and 2022, age and family unit in 2021 and 2023, and the 1968 identifiers. It contains 27,295 people.
The 2023 Parent Identification File from the packaged data, which gives, for every child in the study, the identifiers of the biological mother and father. It has 103,725 rows, and identifies a mother for 60,024 of them and a father for 53,488.

A person in the PSID is identified by two numbers, not one: the 1968 interview number of the household they were born into, and their person number within it. Person numbers restart in every household, so a join on the person number alone would match thousands of unrelated people. Every join below is therefore on the pair.
Matching is done in DuckDB, an in-process analytical database, so the whole parent-child match is expressed as SQL run from Python rather than as row-by-row code. Three steps do the work:

Join. parent_links is joined to the individual file twice, once to the mother and once to the father, and the two results are combined with UNION ALL. Each row of the result is one child-parent pair.
Aggregate. A GROUP BY on the child collapses the pairs back to one row per child, and AVG() combines the incomes of whichever parents qualify.
Filter inside the aggregate. The eligibility rules live in CASE expressions inside the AVG(), so that ineligible parents are treated as NULL and skipped, rather than being averaged in as zeros.

The most important eligibility rule is that the parent must live in a different household from the child. If they lived together, the “parent income” and the “child income” would be the same family income by construction, and the regression would be measuring nothing but the fact that one number equals another.
The final sample is children aged 25 to 55 in 2023, with positive income for both themselves and the matched parent.

title: How Much of a Parent’s Success Does a Child Inherit? Matching Parents and Children with SQL
section: 1. Matching parents to children with SQL
text:
1. Matching parents to children with SQL
The matching pipeline narrows a large panel down to a few thousand usable parent-child pairs, and it is worth following where the observations go.
The parent identification file starts with 103,725 rows, but only 23,938 of them can be joined to a parent who is actually present in the 2023 individual file with a recorded income. That yields 15,728 distinct children with at least one matched parent, of whom 8,210 have both a mother and a father matched and the rest have only one.
Requiring a matched parent with positive income cuts the pool further, to 4,893 children for the single-year measure and 4,139 for the two-year measure, since the two-year average needs both years to be present. Adding the age restriction and positive child income leaves the final regression sample of 3,167 children.
Two features of this design are worth flagging, because they are where a parent-child match usually goes wrong. First, the join is on the pair of identifiers, never on a single one. Second, parents living with the child are excluded inside the aggregate, so a child is never compared with a parent whose household income is mechanically identical to the child’s own.

title: How Much of a Parent’s Success Does a Child Inherit? Matching Parents and Children with SQL
section: 2. One year of income is a noisy signal
text:
2. One year of income is a noisy signal
A single year’s family income mixes two very different things: where a family stands permanently, and whether they happened to have a good or a bad year. Bonuses, overtime, unemployment spells, illness, and a divorce that changes household composition all move measured income without moving economic status. The child’s own income at 25 is even noisier than the parent’s, because a twenty-five-year-old’s earnings are mostly a function of where they are on their career ramp rather than of their eventual position.
Two regressions on the same 3,167 children isolate the effect of measurement alone: one uses only 2022 income, the other averages 2020 and 2022.

    IGE = num(ige),

    `R-squared` = num(r_squared)

Measuring income over two years instead of one raises the estimated IGE from 0.275 to 0.305, and raises the R-squared from 0.073 to 0.092. Both moves point the same way, and the reason is mechanical rather than mysterious. Because a child’s income appears on the left-hand side and the parent’s on the right-hand side, a transitory shock in either household pushes the estimate toward zero: it attenuates the relationship. Averaging two years shrinks the transitory component on both sides at once, so more of what is left is genuine economic status, and the regression has more real signal to work with.
The implied magnitude is easy to state: a 10% higher parental income is associated with roughly a 30.5% higher income for the child. That is a meaningful but far from complete transmission of advantage across generations.

title: How Much of a Parent’s Success Does a Child Inherit? Matching Parents and Children with SQL
section: 3. When you measure a child matters
text:
3. When you measure a child matters
The second source of bias is timing. A child’s income is not a fixed characteristic; it moves through a career. Early in the life cycle, earnings are still climbing steeply, so a bad year or a career break depresses measured income far below where the child will eventually settle. Late in the life cycle, earnings plateau and then often fall, and measured income again drifts away from long-run status. In both cases, the measurement error is not classical noise that averages out of a large sample. It is correlated with the child’s age, and it pushes the estimate toward zero precisely in the groups where the measurement is worst.
To see this, the same regressions are run separately by the child’s age in 2023.

The profile is not flat. Under the two-year measure the estimated IGE rises from 0.340 for children aged 25-34 to a peak of 0.367 for children aged 35-44, then falls back to 0.311 for the oldest group. The single-year measure follows the same shape, peaking at 0.316 in the middle group.
The middle of the range is where the measurement works best. Earnings in the mid-thirties to mid-forties are close to their peak, so current income is a fair proxy for long-run economic status and the attenuation is smallest. At both ends of the range, measured income is a worse proxy for status, and the estimate falls with it. This is the shape that the lifecycle literature warns about, and if it holds it has a direct practical consequence: an IGE measured on young adults will understate the true intergenerational persistence of income.
It is important not to read more into the numbers than they support. The confidence intervals overlap substantially. The 95% interval for the oldest group, [0.225, 0.396], contains the point estimates of both younger groups, and the same is true between the two younger groups. The differences across age groups are therefore suggestive rather than conclusive: the pattern is what the lifecycle story predicts, but this cross-section does not establish it on its own. A larger sample, or the same people followed over their working lives, would be needed to separate the age effect from sampling noise.
One caveat belongs with this result. These are age groups in a single cross-section, not the same people followed over time, so the pattern mixes an age effect with a cohort effect. Children aged 45-55 in 2023 were in their twenties during the 1990s, and children aged 25-34 were in theirs during the 2010s; they entered the labour market under very different conditions. Part of the decline in the oldest group may therefore be cohort-specific rather than a purely mechanical consequence of measuring income too late in life.

title: How Much of a Parent’s Success Does a Child Inherit? Matching Parents and Children with SQL
text:
Limitations

Two years is not a long run. Averaging 2020 and 2022 reduces but does not remove measurement error, which is one reason the R-squared stays near 0.092. The estimates preferred in the literature use much longer income windows, and they are typically larger.
Family income, not individual income. The PSID family income measure includes a spouse’s earnings. A parent’s measure is therefore household income in the parent’s own household, and a child’s measure is household income in the child’s household.
2020 and 2022 are unusual years. They contain the pandemic and its immediate aftermath, when labour markets and household composition moved sharply. The two-year average spans some of that, but not all of it.
Selection. The sample contains children who are observed in 2023 with positive income and whose parent is separately observed. Children who left the study, or who are not separately observed, do not appear, and their absence is unlikely to be random.
No controls. These are single-variable log-log regressions. Adding parental characteristics and child background would change the coefficient from a measure of rank persistence into a structural parameter, which is a different and more ambitious object.
Cross-sectional age profiles. As noted, the age pattern above is a profile of different cohorts, not a panel tracking the same people, and the confidence intervals across age groups overlap. The age pattern is consistent with lifecycle attenuation bias without proving it.

title: How Much of a Parent’s Success Does a Child Inherit? Matching Parents and Children with SQL
text:
Takeaway
Roughly 30% of the income advantage a parent holds is passed on to the child, using two years of income to measure both: an IGE of 0.305, against 0.275 when a single year is used. The gap between those two numbers is not a detail of the data. It is the difference between measuring where a family currently stands and measuring where it stands once temporary luck has washed out.
The age profile points in the same direction. Measured persistence looks weakest where income is measured worst, at the start and end of a career, and strongest in the middle, where income is closest to its plateau, though with overlapping confidence intervals this is a suggestive pattern rather than a settled one. The practical point stands regardless: anyone who reports an intergenerational elasticity without saying how income was measured and at what age is reporting a number that could easily be a third too small.
For policy, the reading is sobering but not fixed. If persistence is this high, then the economic starting point of a child’s parents does substantial work in determining where the child ends up, and the returns to interventions that raise the bottom of the distribution are correspondingly large.
Code and data: github.com/Peterjianghaowen/blog6-sql-ige. Data source: Panel Study of Income Dynamics, Institute for Social Research, University of Michigan.

title: How Much Life Does an Extra Dollar Buy? The Health-Income Curve in 154 Countries
text:
The question
Every government publishes a GDP per capita number and a life expectancy number, but the two are almost never read against each other across countries. Read together, they produce a price. The Preston curve plots life expectancy against log GDP per capita for all countries in a given year, and its slope answers a plain question: if a country’s income doubles, how many more years of life does it buy?
Two things make the curve worth watching over time. First, the slope has been strikingly stable: about 4.7 years of life per doubling of income for three decades. Stability turns the curve into a measuring instrument, because if the price of income is roughly constant, then any movement of the whole curve is a change in the technology of survival — medicine, sanitation, nutrition, vaccination — that income does not capture. Second, the curve has been moving, and it has been moving faster at the bottom of the income distribution than at the top.

title: How Much Life Does an Extra Dollar Buy? The Health-Income Curve in 154 Countries
text:
Data and method
The data come from the World Bank Indicators API (CC BY 4.0), three indicators for every country from 1990 to 2023: life expectancy at birth (SP.DYN.LE00.IN), GDP per capita at PPP in constant 2021 international dollars (NY.GDP.PCAP.PP.KD), and population (SP.POP.TOTL). The panel keeps 154 countries over 1990–2023 (5,081 country-years) after dropping World Bank aggregates, country-years missing any indicator, and countries with fewer than one million inhabitants, whose life expectancy is estimated from small numbers and swings wildly between years.
The method is deliberately simple. Life expectancy is regressed on log2(GDP per capita) separately in each year; the slope is the price of income. The fitted curve is then read off at $5,000 and $40,000 to measure how it moved over time. For the pandemic, each country’s actual 2019–2021 change is compared with its own 2010–2019 pace, annualised and projected across the two pandemic years, so that the comparison is not contaminated by the two windows having different lengths.

title: How Much Life Does an Extra Dollar Buy? The Health-Income Curve in 154 Countries
text:
1. What an extra dollar buys
Fitting the curve year by year gives a median slope of 4.67 years of life per doubling of income, and 4.63 in a pooled model with year effects. The fit is good — R² runs from 0.68 in 1990 to 0.78 in 2023 — so income explains most, but far from all, of the cross-country spread in life expectancy.
The residual is the interesting part. Around the line sit countries that reach far more, or far less, life expectancy than their income predicts: not necessarily rich or poor countries, but countries whose health outcomes are out of line with their material circumstances.

3. The interactive view: the curve, one year at a time
A static scatter plot of the 2019 cross-section answers one question — where do countries sit relative to income this year — and answers it well. It is close to useless for the question I actually care about, which is how the relationship moves. So the main figure below is an interactive one: the cross-section is animated from 1990 to 2023, with the fitted curve re-drawn for every year.


Code

  left_join(region_table, by = "region") |>

  color = ~region_short, frame = ~year,

The legend switches regions on and off, which separates the question “how does income relate to life expectancy” from “is the Sub-Saharan African cluster tight or is it scattered”, and the answer is visibly not tight. The hover tooltips name every country and report its life expectancy, GDP per capita, population, region and income group, so any point in the cloud can be identified and checked. Bubble area is proportional to population, so the reader can see that the countries that matter for most of the world’s people are not the ones sitting furthest from the line.

title: How Much Life Does an Extra Dollar Buy? The Health-Income Curve in 154 Countries
section: 5. Who is above and below the curve
text:
5. Who is above and below the curve
Residuals are taken from a pooled regression with year fixed effects, so each country is compared with what other countries were achieving in the same year rather than with a global average that ignores the curve’s own movement. The twelve largest positive and negative residuals over 1990–2023 are in results/outliers.csv; the largest gaps are Albania (8.94 years), West Bank and Gaza (8.44 years) and China (8.38 years) on one side, and Nigeria (15.65 years), Eswatini (15.55 years) and Equatorial Guinea on the other. Every one of the twelve countries below the curve is in Sub-Saharan Africa.

Income is not the same thing as health. A country can be healthy for reasons that are not in its income — a strong public health system, a diet, a low violence rate — and that is visible in the residuals, which are large, stable over three decades, and concentrated in a handful of countries with recognizable stories behind them.

title: How Much Life Does an Extra Dollar Buy? The Health-Income Curve in 154 Countries
text:
Robustness
Seven of the 5,081 country-year observations are acute mortality crises rather than informative points on the income–health relation: Rwanda in 1994 (12.2 years of life), Somalia in 1991–93, and the Central African Republic in 2009, 2019 and 2022. They are genuine observations and they stay in the main analysis, but the headline numbers were re-estimated without them. The median slope moves from 4.67 to 4.61, the shift at $5,000 from 5.09 to 5.58 years, and the pandemic losses are unchanged to two decimals. The conclusions do not depend on the crisis years.

title: How Much Life Does an Extra Dollar Buy? The Health-Income Curve in 154 Countries
text:
Limitations

The curve is cross-sectional. It describes what countries at a given income achieve, not what happens to a country when its income changes, so it is not a causal return on income.
Life expectancy is a population average. It says nothing about inequality within a country.
Income groups are the current classification applied to all years, so a country that moved between groups is counted in its present group throughout.
The pandemic window is short. Some of the 2021 “excess loss” is catch-up rather than permanent loss, and a longer window would spread the same total over more years.

title: How Much Life Does an Extra Dollar Buy? The Health-Income Curve in 154 Countries
text:
Takeaway
Income buys life, and the price has been remarkably stable: about 4.67 years per doubling, every year, for thirty years. The interesting part is what happens around that price. The curve has been drifting upward underneath it — faster at the bottom, so a poor country gained about 5.09 years between 1990 and 2019 where a rich one gained 3.47 — which is what it looks like when public health technology improves faster than income grows. And then the pandemic took it all back for two years, everywhere, with the middle-income countries losing the most against their own trend.
None of this says that income stops mattering. The slope is still about 4.7 years per doubling. What the analysis adds is the size of the residuals: some countries live many years more, and some many years less, than their income predicts. Income is the price of health, but it is not the whole bill.

title: Are NBA Salaries Efficient? Scraping Stats and Contracts to Find Mispriced Players
text:
The question
Under the salary cap, every dollar a team spends on one player is a dollar it can’t spend on another. So the useful question for a front office is not who the best players are, but who delivers the most production per dollar. If salaries tracked on-court value closely, there would be no bargains to find. This post tests that: I scrape a full season of player statistics and salaries, estimate what the league pays for production, and measure how far each player sits from that rate.

title: Are NBA Salaries Efficient? Scraping Stats and Contracts to Find Mispriced Players
Are NBA Salaries Efficient? Scraping Stats and Contracts to Find Mispriced Players
text:
Method
Production is measured by VORP (value over replacement player), a box-score estimate of a player’s total contribution above a freely available replacement.
To get a market rate, I regress log salary on VORP using only players aged 25 and over. Most of them signed their current deals in free agency, while many younger players are on rookie-scale contracts whose pay is set by draft position rather than negotiated. Applying this curve to every player gives a market value: roughly what a veteran with the same production earns. Surplus value is market value minus actual salary. Predictions are converted back to dollars with Duan’s smearing estimator and capped at the league’s highest salary, since no contract can exceed the max.

title: Are NBA Salaries Efficient? Scraping Stats and Contracts to Find Mispriced Players
section: What a front office should do with this
text:
What a front office should do with this
First, surplus is concentrated in rookie-scale contracts, which makes draft picks the cheapest source of production in the league. A team trying to contend should value its picks accordingly and plan its window around when those players are still on rookie deals.
Second, the biggest overpayments are long contracts that run into players’ 30s. The age premium means teams are still paying for past performance, so shorter terms or declining salary structures reduce that risk.
Third, the undrafted and second-round group is the one source of surplus not created by rookie-scale rules. Scouting outside the lottery for productive players on minimum deals is where a disciplined team can still find value that other teams miss.

title: Are NBA Salaries Efficient? Scraping Stats and Contracts to Find Mispriced Players
text:
Limitations
VORP accumulates with playing time, and teams may give expensive players more minutes than their performance warrants; Staw and Hoang (1995) found this kind of sunk-cost effect for draft position in the NBA. That inflates the measured production of expensive players, so the surplus of cheap players is probably understated. Age is also only a proxy for contract type, and a single season is a noisy sample.

title: Are NBA Salaries Efficient? Scraping Stats and Contracts to Find Mispriced Players
text:
Takeaway
NBA salaries follow current production only loosely, and the gap is systematic: the league underpays young players because rookie contracts are fixed by rule, and overpays veterans for what they used to do. For a team working under a fixed cap, the cheapest wins are the ones it drafts or finds outside the first round.

title: Did Brexit Leave the UK Behind? Output, Investment, and Trade Against the G7
text:
The question
In June 2016 the UK voted to leave the European Union. It formally left in January 2020 and exited the single market and customs union at the end of that year. Ten years after the vote, economists still disagree about what it cost. The difficulty is that we never observe the UK that stayed.
This post takes a simple approach to that problem. I compare the UK with the other six G7 economies, before and after the referendum, on three measures where Brexit should show up if it mattered: output, investment, and trade. If the UK tracked its peers before 2016 and fell behind afterwards, that is evidence consistent with a Brexit cost. If it did not, the simple story needs rethinking.

title: Did Brexit Leave the UK Behind? Output, Investment, and Trade Against the G7
text:
Data and method
The data come from the World Bank’s World Development Indicators, downloaded with the WDI package in R for the seven G7 countries from 2000 to 2025. I use three indicators:

Real GDP per capita (NY.GDP.PCAP.KD, constant 2015 US dollars)
Gross fixed capital formation as a share of GDP (NE.GDI.FTOT.ZS)
Trade, exports plus imports, as a share of GDP (NE.TRD.GNFS.ZS)

Raw levels are not comparable across these countries, so each series is transformed before plotting.

GDP is measured per capita and in real terms, then indexed to 2016 = 100. Per capita matters because population growth differs across the G7, and indexing puts every country on the same scale in the referendum year.
Investment and trade shares are shown as the change in percentage points since 2016. Germany trades a far larger share of its GDP than the United States does, so comparing levels would mostly show country size. Comparing changes shows who moved.

The comparison group is the unweighted average of Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, and the United States. I keep only years in which all seven countries report data, so the average never changes composition. This is why investment and trade end in 2024.
This is a descriptive comparison and not a causal estimate. The G7 average stands in for what might have happened to the UK without Brexit, and the limitations section discusses how well it does that job.

title: Did Brexit Leave the UK Behind? Output, Investment, and Trade Against the G7
section: 1. Output: a gap that opened after exit, not after the vote
text:
1. Output: a gap that opened after exit, not after the vote

The referendum itself left no visible mark on output. In 2019, three years after the vote, the UK index stood at 104.3 against 104.1 for its peers.
The gap appears in 2020. The UK’s pandemic recession was deeper, leaving it 4.8 points behind. It recovered part of that ground by 2022, when the gap narrowed to 1.4 points, and then fell back again. In 2025 real GDP per capita was 5.5% above its 2016 level in the UK and 9.0% above in the peer group, a shortfall of 3.4 points. Among the seven countries, the UK ranks 5 out of 7 for growth since 2016.
Is a gap of that size unusual? Not by itself. Because every country is set to 100 in 2016, the chart also shows relative growth before the referendum: between 2011 and 2016 the UK outgrew its peers by 3.2 points. Swings of this size have happened before, in the UK’s favour. What stands out now is the direction and the persistence: the shortfall was 3.1 points in 2023, 3.6 in 2024, and 3.4 in 2025, well after pandemic restrictions ended.

title: Did Brexit Leave the UK Behind? Output, Investment, and Trade Against the G7
text:
2. Investment: a recovery that stalled

Investment is where economists expected the referendum to bite first, because firms facing uncertainty about future market access tend to postpone spending. The data fit that story, with a caveat.
By 2024 the peer group’s investment share was 1.4 percentage points above its 2016 level. The UK’s was 0.1 points above, essentially unchanged. A gap was already visible in 2019 (0.6 points) and has stayed between 1 and 2 points since 2020.
The caveat is that the two lines were far from parallel before 2016. UK investment had been climbing out of a deep post-crisis trough: its share of GDP rose 2.4 points between 2011 and 2016 while the peer average was flat. The honest reading is that UK investment did not fall after the referendum. A recovery stopped, at the moment when investment in comparable economies began to rise. Note also that this indicator covers all fixed investment, including housing and government, and not business investment alone.

title: Did Brexit Leave the UK Behind? Output, Investment, and Trade Against the G7
text:
3. Trade: the weakest evidence

Trade should give the cleanest test, since leaving the single market raised trade barriers on a known date. The timing does line up. Through 2019 the UK’s trade share had risen faster than its peers’, by 2.7 points, plausibly because the fall in sterling after the referendum raised the pound value of both imports and exports. In 2021, the first year outside the single market, the gap flipped to 3.1 points behind, and it was 1.8 points behind in 2024.
But the UK series is volatile, and that undermines the result. In 2015, before any of this, the UK was already 4.2 points below the peer average on the same measure. The post-2021 gap sits inside the range of gaps seen before the referendum. The direction is what a Brexit effect would predict, but on annual trade shares I cannot distinguish it from ordinary noise. The spike in 2022 across both lines likely reflects energy prices, which raise the nominal value of imports everywhere.

title: Did Brexit Leave the UK Behind? Output, Investment, and Trade Against the G7
text:
Limitations

Other shocks hit at the same time. The UK left the single market in the middle of a pandemic and one year before an energy crisis to which its gas-dependent economy was especially exposed. A comparison with peers cannot separate these from Brexit.
The G7 average is an imperfect counterfactual. The investment and trade charts show that the UK did not move in parallel with its peers before 2016, so some of the later divergence may have happened anyway. A synthetic control that weights countries to match the UK’s pre-2016 path would be the natural next step.
Annual data hide timing. Events such as the referendum in June and the end of the transition period in December fall inside single observations.
Trade shares are nominal. They move with exchange rates and commodity prices as well as with trade volumes.

title: Did Brexit Leave the UK Behind? Output, Investment, and Trade Against the G7
text:
Takeaway
Three charts give three different strengths of answer. Output gives the clearest signal: the UK kept pace with the G7 for three years after the referendum, then fell about 3 points behind after it actually left and has not recovered the ground. A swing of similar size, in the UK’s favour, occurred in the five years before the referendum, so this alone is not proof. Investment points the same way, as a recovery that stalled while peers’ investment rose. Trade does not settle anything at this level of aggregation.
The broader lesson is about timing. The damage many expected from the vote itself does not appear in output. What the data show is a slower divergence that began once the new trading arrangements took effect, which is also when it became hardest to tell apart from everything else that went wrong in 2020.
